newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urges Hun Sen to to end Cambodia fighting.
newsitem.headline: Japan urges Hun Sen to to end Cambodia fighting.

text.p: Cambodia's biggest aid donor Japan urged Second Prime Minister Hun Sen on Sunday to take the lead in ending fighting that has broken out in the country.

"Our nation is deeply concerned that the Cambodian situation had worsened. We strongly urge Second Prime Minister Hun Sen to take the initiative towards a peaceful resolution," Japanese Foreign Minsiter Yukihiko Ikeda said in a statement.

Fighting between troops loyal to Cambodia's rival prime ministers broke out on Saturday when Hun Sen ordered a crackdown on "illegal troops" under Ranariddh's command. The fighting intensified on Sunday with shelling and small arms fire rocking the capital. Explosions were heard in the city centre, near the palace and government buildings, a Reuters reporter said.
The Cambodian Red Cross said on Sunday that there had been 52 casualties from the fighting although it did not give a breakdown on the number of deaths or wounded.
Among those critically wounded was a Japanese engineer, Takamasa Okajima, whose office-home was hit by a rocket on Saturday.
Ranariddh late on Saturday claimed sole legimate power and accused his rivals of attempting a coup.
"We consider that what is currently happening in Phnom Penh is a coup d'etat perpetuated by (second Prime Minister) Mr Hun Sen," said a statement released in Paris in the name of Ranariddh.

In a second statement issued hours later in Paris, where he was said to be visiting family, Ranariddh declared he had become head of Cambodia's only legitimate government as a result of the alleged coup attempt.

"At this time, the sole legitimate government of Cambodia is the one over which I preside, given legitimacy by the free and democratic elections organised by the United Nations in 1993 and by the confidence of the Cambodian people," he said.
The two prime ministers head a deadlocked coalition government set up after United Nations-run elections in 1993.

A long row over power-sharing has been inflamed by deep differences over how to deal with the divided Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, blamed for the deaths of one million people when they ruled in the 1970s and still armed and at large.
Khmer Rouge front man Khieu Samphan said on Sunday that he supported the Cambodian constitution, in effect adding support to Ranariddh, who has been negotiating with the rebels.
